title: Analyzing and Reporting
text:
Journals are free-form notes for recording ideas, decisions and emerging themes as you code. They support reflexivity: being aware of how your own views shape the analysis.

The journal window floats, so you can keep it open beside the coding screen.
Add simple formatting with Markdown: # for headings (up to three levels), *italics* and **bold**. Web links become clickable from the right-click menu.
Search journals, sort them by name or date, filter them, add attributes, and export one journal or all of them as a single file.

Memo vs journal: a memo belongs to one code, file or passage; a journal entry is about the project as a whole.

title: Analyzing and Reporting
section: Retrieving and comparing coded data (Analysis menu)
text:
Retrieving and comparing coded data (Analysis menu)
The Analysis menu turns your coding into evidence. Code retrieval (sometimes called the coding report) is the main tool.

Code retrieval

Choose one or more codes or categories.
Optionally narrow by file, case or attribute, e.g. only second-year students.
Optionally search within results or show only segments marked Important.
Read the matching passages together, then export them as TXT, CSV, XLSX, ODT or HTML.

A matrix view places codes against files or cases, so you can see who talked about what.


Other analysis options



Option
Question it answers




Code co-occurrence
Which codes tend to appear on the same passages?


Code relations
How do two codes sit in the text: overlapping, one inside another, close by, or exactly the same? (Text only)


Codes by text segments
Which codes does each segment carry?


Graph
How do codes and categories connect visually? (See below.)



When you export an HTML report that includes images or media, keep the report’s companion folder with it.

title: Analyzing and Reporting
text:
Reports menu
Reports summarise your project in numbers and charts.

Code frequencies: how often each code was used, by each coder, optionally per file.
File summary / code summary: details about a file or code, including word frequencies (common words removed) and average segment length.
Charts: bar charts, sunbursts, heatmaps, stacked bars and word clouds, opened in your web browser and exportable as HTML.
Coding comparison: compares two coders on the same text using percentage agreement and Cohen’s kappa, a measure of agreement beyond chance. Useful for a class exercise in inter-coder reliability.
Database queries: advanced users can run SQL queries on the project database. Back up first, as queries can change data.







NoteTeaching point



Counting codes is not the same as finding meaning. Frequencies show where to look; reading the passages tells you what they mean.

title: Analyzing and Reporting
section: Visualising codes with the Graph tool
text:
Visualising codes with the Graph tool
The Graph tool draws your categories and codes as a diagram you can rearrange, which helps you see and explain how themes connect.

Choose what to show: all categories or selected ones.
Drag items into position; use the buttons at lower left to space them evenly, and + / – to zoom.
Right-click a code to show its memo or its coded text. Right-click a line to change its thickness, style or colour.
Right-click empty space to add free text boxes, file or case boxes, and extra lines.
Save graphs to reopen later, and export them as PNG, PDF, ODT or draw.io.

A graph exported as PNG is a quick way to include a thematic map in a report or presentation.

title: Working in a team
text:
QualCoder is single-user, so teams use one of two approaches. Either way, give every person a unique coder name (Project > Settings > Change).








Approach
How it works
Best for




Take turns
One person works, closes QualCoder, then passes the zipped project to the next person. Never open the same project at the same time.
Small groups, open (inductive) coding


Master project + merge
Build one master project with all files, give each person a copy, code separately, then merge the copies back. Don’t edit the texts in the copies.
Coding with an agreed codebook (deductive)









Warning



Moving a zipped project through email or cloud storage is fine; running QualCoder on a project inside a synced cloud folder is not.

title: Working in a team
text:
Merging projects
Open the destination project, then use Help > Special functions > Merge projects, choose the source project and run the merge.






Important



Back up the destination project first. Important: There is no undo!



Files, codes and categories that don’t already exist are added.
Coding of text, images and audio/video, plus cases, attributes and journals, is brought across.
Existing attribute values in the destination are not overwritten.
If two people edited the same text file differently, codes may land in the wrong place.

title: Setting Up Your Project
text:
A QualCoder project is a folder ending in .qda that holds everything: a database, your imported files and your coding. A project called “Test” becomes a folder called Test.qda. For our toy project, we will name it “GitHub”.

Choose Project > Create New Project.
Give it a name and choose where to save it.
To share or hand in the project, zip the whole .qda folder.

<FIXME - ADD SCREENSHOT>
The main screen has five tabs: Action log, Manage, Reports, Coding and AI chat. After you change something (for example, add files), use the menu bar to reopen a screen so it refreshes, rather than clicking the tab.
Write a project memo: Adding short memo (about 300–700 characters) describing your research question and data is good practice for future reference and clarity about the project goals and methodology, and the AI tools use it as context. Anything written after a line of ##### is kept private from the AI as we will see in later episodes.
<FIXME: ADD Project memo code block that learners can copy and paste from>






WarningImportant Tips




Save projects on your computer’s own drive, not in a cloud-synced folder or on a USB stick. Syncing while QualCoder is open can corrupt the database.
Keep backup copies in more than one location. You can use cloud storage, USB drives, external hard drives, or a combination of these options for added protection.

section: Bringing in your data: Manage Files
text:
Bringing in your data: Manage Files
All your data comes in through Manage > Manage Files.







Type
Formats




Text
.txt, .docx, .epub, .md, .odt, .pdf, .rtf, .tex


Images
.jpg, .jpeg, .png


Audio and video
.mp3, .m4a, .wav, .mp4, .mov, .ogg (and .wmv video)



<FIXME - ADD SCREENSHOT>
Some other things you can do here:

Create a new text file: and type or paste content directly.
Filter, sort and bulk-rename files, and add attributes to each file.







Caution




QualCoder should not be used for editing, de-identifying, or pseudonymizing raw data. Best practice dictates importing only final, analysis-ready transcripts and notes into the platform for coding.



Let’s import our sample files into QualCoder.
<FIXME - ADD SCREENSHOT>

title: Setting Up Your Project
text:
Cases & Attributes
Cases group data around a person, place or situation. Attributes are the variables that describe them, such as age group or year of study.
Do you need cases? Not always. If each participant has one interview file, you can put attributes straight on the file. Cases help when one person has several files, or when one file (such as a focus group) holds several people.
Working with cases (Manage > Manage Cases):

Add a case, e.g. Participant 01.
Click the case’s Files cell to link whole files, or highlight part of a text and assign just that passage. Linked text is underlined in red.
Add attribute columns and fill in values.
Import attributes from a CSV or XLSX file: first row = column headings, first column = case names. Names must match exactly, including capitals.
Sort, filter or hide columns with a right-click, and export the table to Excel.

Attribute types: QualCoder offers only two:

Character – text values, e.g. “2nd year”.
Numeric – numbers, e.g. 21. You can turn numeric into character later, but not the other way round.

Attributes can be attached to files, cases or journals, and managed in Manage > Manage Attributes. QualCoder is not a statistics package; for statistical analysis of attributes, export them to a tool such as R.
<FIXME: ADD EXERCISE>






NoteWhy this matters for analysis



Attributes will allow you to ask questions like “Do first-year students talk about stress differently from final-year students?”. It allows you to query the data considering demographics and other important characteristics associated with the documents you are analyzing.

title: Setting Up Your Project
text:
References (optional)
If your data includes published articles, you can import a bibliography through Manage > References. This is optional for the workshop but useful for literature reviews.

Import RIS or NBIB files (.ris, .nbib or .txt), or pull references straight from Zotero 7 while it is open with its local API turned on.
Link each reference to its file. The file then gains four attributes: Ref_Authors, Ref_Title, Ref_Type and Ref_Year.
Keep the attributes that start with Ref_; deleting them breaks the link.
Export all references as a RIS file.

title: Meet QualCoder!
text:
QualCoder is a free, open-source desktop program for qualitative data analysis. It helps you organize non-numeric data, such as interviews, documents and images, and tag meaningful passages with codes.
What you can do with it:

Code many kinds of data: text, PDFs, images, audio and video.
Write as you think: keep journals and attach memos to codes, files and coded passages.
Organize ideas: group codes into categories in a tree, like folders.
Analyse and report: retrieve everything tagged with a code, compare codes, and export reports.
Use optional AI tools: search for themes and discuss your data with a large language model. These are switched off by default.

Applications
QualCoder can be used to analyze a wide range of qualitative data files and combine them within the same research project. For example, students can import PDF files such as journal articles, policy documents, reports, or case studies and code them to identify key themes and concepts; audio recordings of interviews or focus groups can be transcribed and coded to explore participants’ experiences, opinions, and perceptions; text files such as open-ended survey responses, interview transcripts, field notes, or meeting notes can be organized into categories and themes; web-based or social-media text can be analyzed to compare public perspectives and discussions; and images or other visual materials such as photographs, screenshots, or field observations can be coded alongside textual data. These different file types can also be combined and compared, allowing students to examine, for example, whether themes identified in policy documents are also reflected in interviews, survey responses, or public discussions.






NoteRound-Robin



How do you envision using QualCoder in your research or coursework? What types of documents or artifacts would you analyze (e.g., journal articles, policy documents, interview recordings, transcripts, survey responses, or images)?


Good to know:

It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and works offline.
It is designed for one person at a time. Teams take turns on a project or merge copies later (see Working in a team).
It aims to follow the REFI-QDA exchange standard, so projects can move to and from tools such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti and MAXQDA, with some limits.
It is licensed under the LGPL v3. If you use it in coursework or research, cite it (the citation is on the QualCoder website).

The simplest route is a ready-made installer from the releases page. Choose the one appropriate for your laptop.








System
What to download
What to expect on first launch




Windows
The Windows installer (.exe)
A SmartScreen warning, because the app is not signed. Click More info, then Run anyway.


macOS
The .dmg file
A Gatekeeper warning. Allow the app under System Settings > Privacy & Security.


Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)
The Linux executable, or run from source
Usually no warning.



Optional extras (which won’t be covered during this workshop)

VLC media player is needed to code audio and video
ffmpeg lets QualCoder draw audio waveforms.

Please note that Audio and video do not work on Fedora Linux.

title: Meet QualCoder!
text:
Basic Settings
Open Project > Settings (or the settings icon). Only four settings matter for a first session.
<FIXME - ADD SCREENSHOT>

Coder name: Every code you apply is stamped with your coder name. Set your own name (or initials) before you start, using the Change button. This matters later if you compare coding with a collaborator.
Language: English is the default. French, German and Spanish are kept up to date; other languages are contributed by volunteers.
Font and display: Increase the font size if text is hard to read on a projector or small screen.
Backups” QualCoder can back up your project every hour and keep the most recent copies, named like projectname_BKP_yyyymmdd_hh.qda. Let’s leave this on!

Behind the scenes: QualCoder keeps its settings file (config.ini) and a log file in a hidden .qualcoder folder in your home directory. Remember: do not store project data there!






TipActivity 1.1 –

title: Coding Data
text:
Coding means attaching a short label (a code) to a passage of data that expresses an idea relevant to your research question. Codes are then grouped into categories, which can grow into themes.








Term
Meaning
Example




Code
A label applied to a passage
Sleep loss


Category
A group of related codes
Physical effects of stress


Coded segment
The passage a code is attached to
“I barely slept the week before finals.”


In vivo code
A code named with the participant’s own words
“running on empty”


Memo
A note explaining your thinking about a code or passage
“Several students link sleep to caffeine use.”



Codes can be planned in advance from theory (deductive) or emerge as you read (inductive). Most student projects mix both.

title: Coding Data
text:
Coding text step by step
Open Coding > Code text. The code tree sits on the left, your document in the center, and the file list nearby.

Create codes and categories

Right-click the code tree and choose to add a new code or category. In the text area, the shortcuts are N (new code) and C (new category).
Right-click a code to rename it, change its color, or add a memo.



Apply a code

Highlight a passage with the mouse.
Click a code in the code tree. The passage takes on the code’s color.

Shortcuts after highlighting: Q reuses your most recent code, R lists recent codes, and V makes an in vivo code from the selected words.


Check and fix your coding

Hover over coloured text to see which code is attached.
To remove a code, click the coded text and press U (or the Unmark button). Ctrl+Z brings back the last code you removed.
To resize a segment, click it and press Shift + arrow to extend or Alt + arrow to shrink.
Where codes overlap, click there and press O to cycle through them.



Add your thinking

Memo a coded segment: hover over it and press M. Memoed text appears in italics.
Annotate any selected text, coded or not, by pressing A. Annotated text turns bold.
Flag a strong example as Important with I. The star button under the code tree then shows only important segments, which is handy for picking quotes.



Auto-coding (use with care!)
Buttons at the top right can code every exact match of a word (case-sensitive; separate options with |, e.g. exam|exams), every sentence containing a fragment, or the section between two markers. Mark speakers creates a code for each speaker in a transcript.






Warning



Auto-coding can be undone only until you close the project, so always review the results.




Handy shortcuts



Key
Action




N / C
New code / new category


Q
Apply most recent code


R
Choose from recent codes


V
In vivo code


U
Remove code at the cursor


Ctrl+Z
Restore last removed code


M
Memo on coded segment


A
Annotate selection


I
Mark as important


S
Search text


B / Shift+B
Set bookmark / jump to bookmark


H
Hide or show the top panel


Ctrl+E
Turn edit mode on or off

title: Coding Data
section: Building and organizing your code tree
text:
Building and organizing your code tree
Your codes live in a tree: categories act like folders, codes sit inside them, and from version 4.0 codes can have sub-codes.
Example tree for the sample research question:

Physical effects of stress (category)

Sleep loss (code)
Eating habits (code)

Coping strategies (category)

Social support (code)

Friends (sub-code)
Family (sub-code)

Time management (code)


Everyday tree tasks (right-click in the code tree):

Move a code into a category, or a category into a larger one.
Merge by dropping one code onto another; their coded segments combine. Don’t drop items on each other unless you mean to merge.
Rename, recolor or memo any code or category. Coding > Color scheme recolors several codes at once and previews how colors look to people with color blindness.
Filter a long tree: F9 shows codes matching some text, F10 shows codes of one color. F11/F12 sort it.
Show coded files: right-click a code to list every passage tagged with it, open each in context, and export them to a text file. This is a quick way to check that a code is used consistently.

A code can belong to only one category. If an idea fits two places, create two similarly named codes.

The Code Organizer
For a bigger clean-up, open the Code Organizer. It shows your codes and categories as a diagram you can restructure: move, merge, rename and remove codes and categories, add new categories, and export the view as a PNG.






Warning



Nothing changes until you click Apply, and once applied the changes cannot be undone. Make a backup first; QualCoder will prompt you to.

title: Coding Data
section: Coding PDFs, images, audio and video (FIXME: REMOVE SINCE WE WONT COVER IT)?
text:
Coding PDFs, images, audio and video (FIXME: REMOVE SINCE WE WONT COVER IT)?
The same idea applies to every data type: choose a code, mark a piece of the data, and add memos where useful.








Data type
How you mark it
Worth knowing




PDF
Select text in the PDF view or in a plain-text view of it
Shortcuts mirror text coding (Q, R, M, A, I). Projects coded in 4.0 may show misaligned codes if opened in 3.8.2 or earlier.


Image
Select a code, then drag a rectangle over part of the image
Right-click to rotate, zoom, or apply grayscale, blur or solarize to see details. Exports to HTML show code names on hover.


Audio / video
Press Start segment / Stop segment (Ctrl+S) while playing, then right-click a code to assign it
Needs VLC. Code the transcript text too, and link text to segments. Change play speed from 0.1x to 2x.



In all three, you can mark items as Important, attach memos, and use the star button to show only important items.
Useful audio/video shortcuts: Ctrl+P play/pause, Alt+R rewind 30 seconds, Ctrl+Shift+< and > slow down or speed up playback.

TipActivity 3.2

title: Introduction to Qualitative Data Analysis with QualCoder
text: In this 3 hour workshop, attendees with no QualCoder experience will set up a project, code real qualitative data, and pull out a first report.

title: Introduction to Qualitative Data Analysis with QualCoder
text:
Learning outcomes
By the end, participants will be able to:

Explain what QualCoder is and what kinds of data it handles.
Create a project and import text, PDF, image or audio/video files.
Set up cases and attributes to describe participants.
Create codes and categories, and apply them to text.
Write memos and journal entries to record analytic thinking.
Retrieve coded segments and produce a simple report.
Describe what QualCoder’s optional AI tools do, and the ethical questions they raise.

title: Under the hood
text:
Built with: Python 3 and Qt6. Development happens openly on GitHub, inspired by the earlier R package RQDA.
Project structure: a .qda folder contains a SQLite database plus imported files, and an ai_data folder if AI is enabled. Settings and logs live in the hidden .qualcoder folder in your home directory.
Database: the docs describe each table (files, cases, codes, coded text, attributes, journals and more) for people who want to write SQL queries. Text positions are counted in characters; audio and video positions in milliseconds.
Licence: LGPL v3, so QualCoder is free to use, share and modify.
Contributing: anyone can help by translating the interface or the docs, or by contributing code via GitHub. Documentation lives as Markdown files in the qualcoder-org.github.io repository.
AI technical information: this page of the official docs is still a placeholder.

title: AI Features
text:
QualCoder’s AI tools are off by default and entirely optional. In this workshop they are a facilitator demo, not a student task.



Run the setup wizard (shown after a fresh install, or via AI > Setup Wizard).
Turn on AI integration and choose a model. Options include commercial models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) with an API key, university-hosted services, other providers such as Mistral or OpenRouter, or a local model via Ollama, which keeps data on your computer.
Wait while QualCoder builds a local “AI memory” of your documents. It downloads an embedding model of about 2.5 GB once, and the status bar shows AI: reading until it is ready.





QualCoder sends only short, selected chunks of text (around 500 characters each) to a cloud model, not whole documents.
Anything in a memo after a ##### line is never sent to the AI.
Anonymise data before using any cloud service, and check what your ethics approval allows.

Prepare the project: a clear project memo, readable file names, and labelled speakers in transcripts all improve AI results.

title: AI Features
text:
AI-assisted coding and AI chat
AI-assisted coding searches your data by meaning, not exact words. You pick a code (or type a free topic), choose an analytic prompt, and optionally filter by documents, cases or attributes. QualCoder first searches its local memory, then asks the language model to rank and explain the best matches. You review each suggestion and decide whether to code it. The docs stress this is assisted, not automated, coding.
AI chat offers four kinds of conversation:







Chat type
What it does




Topic analysis
Explores a theme across all your data, even before you’ve coded


Text analysis
Discusses a selected passage: brainstorm, summarise, suggest themes, or look for the unexpected


Code analysis
Sends everything under one code or category for a summary or comparison; watch the cost on large codes


General chat
Open conversation about your project



Prompt library: the instructions sent to the AI are plain-language prompts you can view, copy and edit via AI > Prompt library. Built-in system prompts must be duplicated before editing. Prompts are in English but work with data in other languages.

title: AI Features
text:
Demo and discussion






TipDemo 5.1 – AI-assisted coding (5 min, facilitator)




What to show: e.g. run AI-assisted coding for the code Social support on the sample data; accept one suggestion, reject one
Model used: e.g. local Ollama model / institutional service
Backup plan if the AI is slow: e.g. screenshots or a pre-recorded clip









TipDiscussion 5.1 – Should we use AI here? (5 min)




Prompt 1, e.g. “What did the AI find that you missed? What did it get wrong?”
Prompt 2, e.g. “Who is responsible for an interpretation suggested by AI?”
Prompt 3, e.g. “Would your participants have agreed to their words being sent to an AI company?”
Course policy note: insert your institution’s or course’s AI-use policy

title: Episodes
text:
Each episode explains one stage of a QualCoder project and ends with hands-on activities.



Episode
Time
You will learn to




1 – Meet QualCoder

Install QualCoder and set your coder name


2 – Set Up Your Project

title: Imports and exports
text:
Most options are under the Project menu.

Codebook: export or import codes as plain text or CSV. In the plain-text format, >> puts a code under a category and >>> puts a code under another code; a memo follows after a tab (or in the second CSV column).
REFI-QDA: exchange whole projects or codebooks with other QDA software such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA and Quirkos. QualCoder does not meet the standard fully, so some items (such as sets and graphs) may not transfer. Close any open project before importing.
Other tools: import projects from Taguette, Sonal Pi and RQDA.
If imported coding seems missing, change your coder name in Settings to match the original coder.

title: Imports and exports
text:
Survey imports
Open-ended survey responses can be imported from CSV or XLSX through Manage > Manage Files > Import survey.

Row 1 holds the column headings.
One column holds a unique ID, which becomes the case.
Short answers (age, gender) become attributes. A column becomes Numeric only if every value is a number or blank.
Free-text answers become text files, one per case, ready to code.
More columns can be added for the same cases later, or existing values replaced, by importing another file with the same IDs.
Very large surveys (1,000+ rows) can take a while to import.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
Code of Conduct
This workshop is a welcoming space for everyone, whatever their background or experience with research software.
We expect participants to:

Be respectful and patient with one another, especially during pair work.
Treat all workshop data as confidential, even when it is fictional practice data.
Ask questions freely; there are no silly questions in a first session.

Unacceptable behaviour includes harassment, discriminatory language, and sharing others’ data or work without permission.
Reporting: contact the facilitator at [facilitator email] or [your institution’s reporting channel].
Adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1.
